outputs.L2: The system includes a magnetic core and an electrical coil. An electromagnetic actuator comprises a magnetic core and an electric coil that work together to convert electrical energy into mechanical energy. When an electric current is supplied to the coil, a magnetic field is generated. This magnetic field acts on the magnetic core and causes it to move. The movement of the magnetic core provides the mechanical force required for actuation.

This mechanical movement is used by the electromagnetic actuator to operate a valve. In particular, the displacement of the magnetic core is transmitted to a valve body, causing the valve body to move between different operating positions, such as an open position and a closed position. In this way, the actuator controls the flow of a fluid through the valve.

A controller is provided to monitor and evaluate the operation of the electromagnetic actuator. During operation, the controller measures the current flowing through the electric coil. The measured current forms a current course over time, which reflects the electrical behavior of the coil and can also indicate the mechanical response of the actuator.

To assess the actuator condition, the controller selects a temporal evaluation section within the measured current course. This evaluation section has a defined duration and includes a beginning point and an end point. The controller evaluates the current value at the beginning of the selected section and the current value at the end of the selected section.

Based on these current values and the duration of the selected evaluation section, the controller determines an evaluation product. The evaluation product is then compared with a predefined limit value. If the evaluation product deviates from the expected range or exceeds or falls below the predefined limit, the controller detects an error or malfunction of the electromagnetic actuator. Such an error may indicate, for example, that the magnetic core or valve body is not moving correctly, that the actuator is mechanically blocked, or that the electromagnetic response of the actuator differs from the intended behavior. Thus, by monitoring the current course and evaluating a selected temporal section, the controller can reliably identify actuator errors during operation.

An electromagnetic actuator for moving a valve body comprises a magnetic core, an electric coil assigned to the magnetic core, and an armature or other movable element coupled to the valve body. When the coil is energized, a magnetic field is generated in the magnetic core, causing the movable element to shift and thereby move the valve body between different operating positions. Such an actuator may be used, for example, in a valve arrangement in which reliable opening and closing behavior must be monitored during ongoing operation.

To improve fault detection, the actuator is connected to a controller that monitors the electrical behavior of the coil. During operation, the controller detects or receives current values of the coil current and evaluates a selected time section of the current profile. This time section may be chosen from a phase in which the coil is energized, de-energized, or otherwise driven in a defined manner. The current value at the beginning of the selected time section, the current value at the end of the selected time section, and the duration of the selected time section are determined.

From these values, the controller forms an evaluation product. The evaluation product is based on the current value at the start of the time section, the current value at the end of the time section, and the length of time between them. The result therefore represents a characteristic feature of the current curve over the selected interval. Because the current profile of an electromagnetic actuator is influenced by the magnetic circuit, the movement of the armature, and the mechanical behavior of the valve body, deviations in this evaluation product can indicate abnormal actuator operation.

The controller compares the evaluation product with a predefined limit value. If the evaluation product exceeds the limit value, falls below the limit value, or otherwise lies outside an allowable range, the controller identifies an actuator error. Such an error may be caused, for example, by a sluggish or blocked valve body, an incorrect armature movement, a mechanical defect, contamination, wear, or an electrical fault affecting the coil or its drive circuit.

By using the relationship between the start current, the end current, and the duration of the evaluated current section, the controller can detect faults without requiring additional position sensors or complex measurement systems. The method therefore provides a simple and robust way to monitor the operational state of the electromagnetic actuator. It allows errors to be recognized during normal operation and can support diagnostic functions, protective shutdowns, warning messages, or fallback strategies in the system in which the valve is installed.

A magnetic core is an essential component used in many electrical and electronic devices to guide and strengthen magnetic fields. It is typically made from materials with high magnetic permeability, such as iron, ferrite, or specialized steel alloys. These materials allow magnetic flux to pass through them more easily than through air, making the device more efficient.

Magnetic cores are commonly found in transformers, inductors, electromagnets, motors, and generators. In a transformer, for example, the magnetic core helps transfer energy between coils by concentrating the magnetic field created by alternating current. This improves power transfer and reduces energy loss.

Different types of magnetic cores are used depending on the application. Laminated steel cores are often used in power transformers to reduce eddy current losses. Ferrite cores are popular in high-frequency devices because they have low electrical conductivity and can operate efficiently at radio frequencies. Powdered iron cores are also used in applications where stability and controlled magnetic properties are important.

The shape of a magnetic core can vary as well. Common forms include toroidal cores, E-cores, U-cores, and rod cores. Each design affects how the magnetic field is distributed and how efficiently the device operates.

In modern technology, magnetic cores play a crucial role in energy conversion, signal filtering, wireless communication, and power management. By improving magnetic performance and reducing losses, a magnetic core helps make electrical systems smaller, more reliable, and more efficient.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a patent-style description of an apparatus including a magnetic core, electric coil, valve body, and controller that evaluates a temporal section of coil current to identify malfunction.
counterfactuals.output:
An apparatus is disclosed for actuating and monitoring a valve. The apparatus includes a magnetic core, an electric coil disposed relative to the magnetic core to generate a magnetic field when energized, a valve body having a movable valve member operatively influenced by the magnetic field, and a controller electrically coupled to the electric coil.

The magnetic core may define a magnetic flux path and may include one or more pole portions arranged to concentrate magnetic flux in a region adjacent the movable valve member. The electric coil may be wound around at least a portion of the magnetic core or otherwise positioned to magnetically excite the core. The valve body may define a fluid passage and a valve seat, and the movable valve member may be configured to move between a first position and a second position to selectively restrict or permit fluid flow through the fluid passage.

The controller is configured to supply an excitation signal to the electric coil and to monitor an electric current flowing through the electric coil during energization. In particular, the controller evaluates a temporal section of the coil current, such as a selected time window occurring after initiation of coil energization, after termination of coil energization, or during a transition between operating states of the valve. The temporal section may include a current rise portion, a current decay portion, a holding-current portion, or a portion in which the current exhibits a change associated with movement of the movable valve member.

The controller determines at least one characteristic of the temporal section of the coil current. The characteristic may include, for example, a slope, curvature, inflection point, peak value, minimum value, time derivative, integral, time to reach a threshold, deviation from a reference profile, or a detected disturbance caused by a change in inductance of the coil as the movable valve member moves. Based on the characteristic, the controller identifies a malfunction of the apparatus.

The malfunction may include sticking of the movable valve member, delayed movement of the movable valve member, failure of the movable valve member to reach an intended position, blockage or restriction in the valve body, abnormal friction, wear, electrical degradation of the coil, a short circuit, an open circuit, deterioration of the magnetic core, or an abnormal supply voltage condition. In some embodiments, the controller compares the evaluated temporal section with stored reference data representative of normal operation. If a deviation exceeds a predetermined threshold, the controller generates a malfunction signal. The malfunction signal may be stored in memory, transmitted to a supervisory control system, used to illuminate a diagnostic indicator, or used to modify operation of the apparatus.

In one embodiment, the controller applies a voltage pulse to the electric coil and samples the coil current at a plurality of sampling instants within a predetermined time interval. The controller isolates the temporal section corresponding to expected motion of the movable valve member and calculates a parameter representative of the current profile within that section. Movement of the valve member changes the magnetic reluctance of the magnetic circuit and thereby modifies the inductance of the coil. This inductance change produces a detectable feature in the coil current. Absence, displacement, attenuation, or distortion of the feature indicates a malfunction.

The apparatus may further include a current sensor arranged to measure the coil current. Alternatively, the controller may determine the coil current indirectly from a voltage across a sense resistor, a switching device, or another circuit element. The controller may include a processor and a memory storing instructions which, when executed, cause the processor to energize the coil, acquire current data, select the temporal section, evaluate the selected section, and determine whether a malfunction is present.

The controller may be configured to compensate the evaluation for temperature, supply voltage, coil resistance, operating pressure, or prior operating history. The reference data may be fixed, learned during a calibration operation, or updated during service. The controller may also classify the malfunction according to a type or severity based on the evaluated temporal section.

Accordingly, the apparatus provides both actuation of the valve and diagnosis of operating condition by analyzing the temporal behavior of the electric current in the coil. This permits malfunction identification without requiring a separate position sensor for the movable valve member.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output:
1. **A valve-operated electromagnetic actuator**, comprising:  

   a valve member movable between a first valve position and a second valve position;  

   an electromagnetic drive unit including a coil and a magnetic circuit having a movable magnetic core operatively coupled to the valve member, the movable magnetic core being displaceable in response to energization of the coil to actuate the valve member; and  

   a controller configured to supply an actuating current to the coil during an actuation period,  

   wherein the controller is further configured to define a time section within the actuation period, determine a first value representative of the actuating current at or near a beginning of the time section, determine a second value representative of the actuating current at or near an end of the time section, analyze a change in the actuating current between the first value and the second value, and detect a faulty operation of the valve-operated electromagnetic actuator based on the analyzed change.

2. The valve-operated electromagnetic actuator of claim 1, wherein the controller is configured to determine a current difference between the second value and the first value and to detect the faulty operation when the current difference satisfies a predetermined fault criterion.

3. The valve-operated electromagnetic actuator of claim 2, wherein the predetermined fault criterion comprises the current difference being less than a threshold value corresponding to insufficient movement of the movable magnetic core.

4. The valve-operated electromagnetic actuator of claim 1, wherein the faulty operation comprises at least one of sticking of the valve member, incomplete displacement of the movable magnetic core, failure of the valve member to reach an intended end position, or abnormal magnetic response of the electromagnetic drive unit.

5. The valve-operated electromagnetic actuator of claim 1, wherein the time section is selected such that movement of the movable magnetic core during normal operation produces a characteristic change in the actuating current.

6. The valve-operated electromagnetic actuator of claim 1, wherein the controller is configured to detect the faulty operation without requiring a separate position sensor for detecting a position of the movable magnetic core or the valve member.
